text:
I've been on a search for a good, under $20, pasta option for a little while. Bar One isn't it.

     Let's start with what it is, though. Can you go have a beer with your friends, and watch a little of the game? Yes, you definitely can. Do they have a beer list which comparable to other crafty, Philly spots? Yes, definitely. Is it crazy expensive, or crazy crowded? Nope...it's ostensibly a neighborhood bar.

     By no stretch of the imagination is it an Italian restaurant. Frankly, I'm not sure why Bar One even bothers to pretend it is such...perhaps the neighborhood, or proximity to the market...but at any rate, fine Italian cuisine it is not. Excited to try a new spot, stopped in on a brisk Friday in November and, ordered the cavatelli with Gorgonzola sauce and sausage. The most notable issue was that there was no sausage. Strike one. I could not identify the flavor of Gorgonzola in the pale grey sauce either. Let it be know that I love blue cheese, and a little goes a long way with said ingredient; it's a strong flavor. This, however, tasted more like a bland rue. The pasta itself was stuck together in clumps, which made me wonder how it was prepared...pasta doesn't do that in a sauté pan.  It was thoroughly underwhelming. 

    It's also worth mentioning the staff...or at least one bartender.  My gent was fine. He seemed to have a little trouble getting around, but was courteous enough, and managed my order with no issues. There was another, much ruder, gent who spent the evening - or at least the time that I was there - trying to recruit customers into belittling the other bartender (the one serving me). "Can you believe he has a degree in music?!?!...in MUSIC?", he asked me with his absurd Thomas Shelby haircut and manicured beard. "Who does that?!?", he continued in his effort to impress himself. I absolutely did not take the bait; nor did most of the other customers, in what I can only expect was everyone trying to extend common kindness to a man just trying to do his job. 

     Let's have a reality check here. 1. Publicly belittling others lacks both character and professionalism. Full stop. 2. I have a degree in music, and what has been (so far, thanks be to God) a lasting & rewarding career in the Arts. So, what was meant only as unnecessary posturing between staff members, deeply offended your clientele. I chose not to engage the argument, because that is in no way what I'm looking for in a dinning experience...an argument with an arrogant, yet poorly-informed bartender. The phrase "service industry" springs to mind...SERVICE...since we like to repeat ourselves. In conclusion, the food was edible but not good; yet it was the utter pretension of Mr. Shelby which will ensure that I will neither spend another singular dollar, nor recommend Bar One to any of my friends or readers. #Service

text:
Ahhh the Lobster Haven... I'm a fan and here's why... Going back to when I used to live in Montreal, Canada, we would always have lobster maybe twice a month.  So from a young age I had the love for them.  Fast forward having lived in NorCal (Bay Area) and SoCal now (Los Angeles County), fresh lobster is not really all that fresh(Maine lobster), I mean, it has to travel next day air if it were really fresh.  So since I am here(business) on the East coast, even though it's southern East coast, I might as well have some lobster from Maine.  Right? That is one of the check boxes in my "to do list".  Just as how I tell my friends from other states, that if you're ever in California, go to a real taqueria (Tsk-tsk for Yelp to have the spell check 'red underline' for the word "taqueria", I'm almost offended here...) yeah so like I was saying, a real taqueria and not some place called Taco John's that I have run into in some states when the locals tell me it's authentic... not that Taco John's is a bad place, hey if that's what you got then, roll with it.  My point is, if you can't get to the source, then at least be in the right time zone, can I get a high five then a chest bump here?!

So back to Lobster Haven, you can have the lobster fresh, or re-fresh.  If you know about seafood, then you know about the differences in freshness.  A little secret for you, sushi grade fish is usually frozen for a brief time to kill off parasites.  You can have it freshly made, if you get it from the fish market when it comes off the boat, then take to your favorite sushi spot and have them go at it for you, but it's custom to let them have some as well since they are doing you the favor.  For lobster, they are shipped 'live' and the packages are ventilated.  Unless they are frozen and then completely boxed.  Shipping in a huge container and temp controlled trucks/semis are the best.  Have you seen the prices for temp controlled next day air?! You'd probably have to own a business that specializes in Lobster.... errr yeah, like lobster haven... LOL... can't believe i just did that merry-go-round- thing with a lobster tangent right back into my review... mad skillz.

Okay, so the current price for the cup of lobster chowda is now $8, which means that it doubled and i guess that's what happens when the season is not as strong or in season.  This is the reason my review is giving a 4 star rating and not a 5.  The price is up there, and that sucks because we always get the bowl of lobster chowda, the lobster roll, and an order of a dozen blue points oysters.  Let me tell you that one order of each will put you into the $50 range with tax and all that rounding off.  So my friend an I ordered a lobster chowda bowl and lobster roll each and then shared the bluepoints oysters.  Pretty much came up to just under $100 after round up, maybe with tax and all that.  It was well worth the money.  I would go there again tomorrow if I lived in the area.  

They also have beers and wines there and I always wanted to try the smoked fish spread but i guess that will have to wait.  The service there has always been very good to us and the wait time for food has never been too bad.  If it's crowded, then a bit of a wait since the staff is only 3 at most I have seen, but grab a beer and go peruse the frozen and fresh section, OMG i saw a huge lobster tail that I dared not ask the price.  Careful though, even though you get a bigger tail, the taste will not be the same.  Now if you have garlic butter, then it doesn't matter, because it will taste buttery good.  Best time to go is either when they open or the off hours like 2pm.  Maybe doing this review was not the best at this time, because now I'm craving it again and I just ate there for lunch today... ahhhh

Imagine, if you will, the most delicious pizza you have ever tasted.  A thin, chewy, slightly charred crust with fresh melty cheese.  Ok.  This was exactly opposite.  

The result of my consumption was a rude, middle of the night wake-up call by my digestive system.  While my body was filled with food, my soul was equally filled with regret.  This was a rookie mistake made by a seasoned veteran.  It would be wrong to advise visitors to downtown Philadelphia to avoid this 7-eleven, but one would be wise to stick to the Big Gulps and go to sleep hungry.

text:
There is a little something for everyone at Lettuce Lake Park.  

We visited yesterday as part of the Hillsborough County Hiking Spree. After paying the two dollar entrance fee we parked in one of the paved parking lots right inside the entrance. From here we had access to the playground, which we visited first for my five-year-olds sake, the paved hiking/biking/jogging loop and the rentable pavilions.

The playground consists of a couple swings and a structure that has lots of slides coming from it. It is pretty standard as far as Hillsborough County Park playgrounds go. What I liked about this one is that the playground is located in a huge open area. So not only can kids swing and slide but they can also run, break out a soccer game, play baseball or any number of other activities that require more space. 

After we were through with the playground, it was time to get our hike on. We started at the paved loop that runs around the entire park. The loop is a pretty easy walk. It has workout equipment at various stops along it. Some of the equipment is pretty obvious as far as what it should be used for (pull up bars, gymnastic rings) and some of it, if you aren't in the know, requires imagination. I've seen some parks that have little signs explaining the different workout areas or offering suggested workouts and I think Lettuce Lake could use that. From the loop there are a number of "trails" that lead off of it. We left the loop to take a look at a circle of cypress trees in the swamp. We also left it to spend time on the boardwalk

The boardwalk is probably the best part of hiking at Lettuce Lake. From the safety of this boardwalk you can look out into the Hillsborough River. Here you will see alligators, birds, turtles and possibly snakes (I've yet to see one but I've heard they are there). My daughter loved the huge lookout tower that is on the boardwalk. The tower is three stories high and provides those that are willing to climb it a spectacular view of the river. 

Lettuce Lake Park is a great place full of fun for everyone who likes outdoor activities. If you are in the USF area and looking for some outdoor time without roughing it too much, Lettuce Lake is the place for you.

Customer service with Gate 1 Travel:  when you've booked your trip and on the trip: POOR.  We were both very sick with bronchitis during our last days (air in Rome, Florence and Venice was covered with thick yellow brown smog). We had a 7:35AM flight to catch for the US from Venice. We bought a voucher with Gate 1 Travel from Venice hotel to Airport. Was to be picked up at 4:40 AM.  We tried to find out if it would be by water taxi or street taxi.  Remember it was freezing cold and damp. Then the Gate 1 Travel documents, section "KNOW BEFORE YOU GO," state on page 18 for Venice. This falsely says that, "after you're dropped off by water taxi, you have to walk 1/2 mile to the airport." We didn't know this was false.  My husband and I were very sick, and called Gate 1 Travel on the last night in Venice to find out about 2 things:  due to the hour of 4:40 AM, will we be using water or street taxi; and how about that 1/2 mile walk.  I tried to find all this out prior to our departure, only to be told nothing by Gate 1 Travel, nor by the Italian transport agency (I called and emailed).  So we called Gate 1 Travel and spoke with supervisor, Jen in Venice on our last night.  My husband wanted information, and Jen was very rude.  All she kept saying was there'd be no refund on the voucher. We didn't ask for one.  Then she lied about the 1/2 mile walk (my concern was darkness, cobblestones, what to expect walking 1/2 mile at 5:00 AM rolling luggage in 35 degree weather). If you have celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity I HIGHLY recommend avoiding this place at all costs. My cousin and I both have celiac disease and went there last night. I ordered fish tacos and she ordered a chicken salad. I checked online about my meal and all ingredients listed were gluten free (I was mainly concerned with the sauce on the fish since I knew the tortillas were corn and the toppings were salad- all gluten free things). My cousin TOLD the waitress she was gluten free and couldn't eat gluten and the waitress said "I got you".  She ordered chicken and salad. When my tacos came out they were fried in flour- does not say fried on the menu but that's fine. I sent them back and apologized for not asking further questions but explained I too have celiac disease and can't have flour and I asked if I could reorder what my cousin was eating since hers looked good and was gluten free. The waitress then says hers was not gluten free and says she didn't hear my cousin say that. My cousin had all but finished her plate by that time so it was only a matter of time before she was sick. She brought out my dinner which was chicken and salad and my chicken was made differently than my cousins was (without soy sauce). And it was really just okay. 

I understand this establishment doesn't claim to be gluten free. However when someone says they are, PAY ATTENTION. Especially since they do offer gluten free items upon request and she said "I got you" as if it wouldn't be an issue. It's a food allergy. Which can kill you over time so it's extremely important to listen. Drinks were good and service overall was decent. I hate that the waitress didn't pay attention though and then tried to say she wasn't told about the allergy when she was- we all heard. Won't be back due to this, which is unfortunate because it seemed like a cool place. If you don't have celiac disease it seems like a good place though!

text:
Bottom Line: A very popular cash only breakfast and brunch eatery in the heart of Philly which serves hearty savory meals and decadent sweet entrees while being environmentally friendly.

My husband and I visited Green Eggs Cafe on a Sunday morning.  We got in line about 7:50am and we were the third party to be seated.  Kudos to Green Eggs for metering out the seating of guests rather than rushing to seat everyone and then the wait staff being overwhelmed and tables underserved. I really appreciated their approach to the morning queue.

Something else that I really liked about Green Eggs was that they serve quality La Colombe coffee.  I decided to order a $3 Diet Coke but had I know the soda refills were going to be an extra $2 I definitely would have opted to have coffee for my morning caffeine. That's been a tough pill to swallow. 

Usually I get a savory breakfast because I like to have protein in the morning to keep me going.  I was tempted to get an omelette, a benedict or The Kitchen
Sink skillet but I decided to veer from my usual and get the Salted Caramel Banana Stuffed French Toast. Our food came out quickly and the French toast presentation was gorgeous!  As much as I have a sweet tooth the French toast was just too sweet for me but it would have been a nice dish to share.

My husband had an omelette without cheese and said it was one of the best omelettes he's ever had!  I feel that is worth repeating . . . an omelette without cheese . . .  one of the best he's ever had!  I snuck a few of his breakfast potatoes and thought they were very tasty.

The restaurant's name is a cute play on words.  They don't serve green eggs and ham as the "green" in their name refers to their "eco-conscious philosophy."  

Speaking of green, bring your greenbacks because they are a cash only business! I'm not sure if they own the ATM and it's an additional revenue for stream for them or if they are just trying to avoid paying credit card fees.

Conveniently, there is a parking lot right across the street but I'm not sure what the rates are.  There is also Indego bike share out front too.

The storefront at Green Eggs is really plain and it would be easy to pass.  An awning or some planters out front would really add some curb appeal.  

If I return I'll definitely go for a savory dish and LaColombe coffee.

text:
Everyone keeps talking about the curse of this corner. Restaurants have come and gone:  Johnny Rockets (terrible); La Salsa (really wasn't bad); Pazzo (some positives, some negatives, just couldn't get a food hold).

So, when I heard that the famously fabulous Crushed Red, home the storied "best salad in St. Louis," was coming to K-wood, I was sure the curse would be Crushed.

Alas, there's some work to do.

First, the positives.  The staff was chipper and cheerful, which is always welcome.
The decor is pleasing, with lots of oversized booths and a few jumbo high top tables to satisfy groups, like my bunch of 8 last night.  The Queen Margarita pizza was tasty, with lots of yummy pesto.  The crust was adequate, in a bready, carby way.

Now, the to-do list. Since I had never been to Crushed Red and the salad/ pizza choices were many, I asked the server for her advice.  She suggested the Margarita pizza or the shrimpy pizza and the Welcome Back Cobbler salad.   She was right on with the pizza, but the Welcome Back Cobbler was absolutely terrible--I hardly ate any of it, and that is way abnormal for this one.  The salads come in three sizes, so I chose the "mini" to go with my pizza.  The size was the only good thing about the salad.  It was swimming with dressing, brimming with a minefield of croutons, dehydrating with its saltiness. Really, it was a pile of mush.  Here's the weird thing.  My pal, Cindy, had a larger version of the salad, and could not have found a crouton to save her soul!  And, her salad seemed properly dressed.  She loved hers.  I hated mine.
Ordering and paying can be quick or onerous, depending on the number of folks in the restaurant.  You start by placing a pizza order, then move through a line to select a salad, continue through the line to grab a beverage (adult or otherwise)  and then pay.  This line bunches up quickly, as there are only two registers.  I did an end run by paying after I placed my salad order and then going back to pick up my salad.  The assembly line aspect doesn't seem to work efficiently.

Friend Kim liked her Farmer's Market salad.  Friends Kati and Christy were already at Crushed Red for the second time.  So, there's hope for Crushed Red on this corner of town.

I think coming here during happy hour would be awesome with substantial price reductions, including $3 off house martinis and I drink vodka ones. $1-$3 of the beers.  Plus it's just a nice place to hang out. So definitely recommended.

We had no appetizers, trying to keep or tab down.  Hubby had the hot chicken with sweet potato pancakes. He liked it although he's not into hot spicy food. Only complaint (mine not his) is throw in a second piece of chicken or a bigger stack of pancakes.

I had three tacos, vampire, pork belly, Korean rib. All three were tasty and the vampire one is the most impression as to presentation. I also opted for flavored rice and beans. Not sure what if any dish the rice represents. Maybe their own creation, but tasty.

I had two shots of the house tequila, which at $5.95 each for a standard shot glass would have liked a little bit more or pricing along the lines of $4 or $4.50 a shot for a shot of house. For $5.95 I can get a well drink on the rocks.


The bartenders were friendly and attentive. I would recommend coming here after work.  It's new, service (at least at the bar) was swift. Food came out quickly. Nicely presented. Portions need to be a little bigger. Prices could come down a dollar or two, but, again, happy hour should solve the price issue.  

Last but not least, we shared a dessert of peach some cobbler with caramel ice cream $3.95...yum.

Boss! One star added for the waitress noticing our dessert hasn't come out after 10 minutes and the manager coming over to explain, apologize, and comp us (we hadn't complained).

Awesome...I hope this kind of service is Madurai maintained!  We'll be back.

text:
"Missed it by that much." The catch phrase from Agent 86 of the TV series "Get Smart" is appropriate for this review. More on that later...

My brother and I grew up in Tucson. He now lives out of state, but when he is home, he is like a moth to a light bulb when he is near a Nico's restaurant. It's almost a pilgrimage to him. To me, I see another "red and yellow" Mexican fast food chain. Kind of like Mexican tire stores. If it's not painted yellow, it's not a llantera. But I digress.

I'd never eaten at a Nico's. Until his recent visit to Tucson. He talked me into it and it wasn't hard. I'm always interested in Mexican food!

First, I want to apologize to him because I was wrong. When you live in Tucson, there are so many other options to fall in love with. Why Nico's? For starters, Nico's menu strongly resembles other chains which all serve the same thing. But for some reason, the simple lunch I enjoyed with him was much better than anticipated.

Obviously, it was freshly prepared just before we dined in the Broadway & Kolb location. The taco was simple, deep fried and tasty. Even the beans had me convinced they were homemade, but I'm not 100% positive on that. The enchilada though just missed the mark. It was flavorful with an above average sauce, but undercooked and a bit soggy. Still, who can reject cheese and tortilla? Not me.

So, my brother opened my eyes and Nico's impressed me. But in the end, the enchilada made the difference cause I wanted to give them four stars. Missed it by that much!

text:
We've heard from a few people that around this area that this place was good.  Since we happened to be in the small town of Souderton we decided to stop in for lunch.  We made a reservation (through Resy), since I hate waiting.  Surprisingly the spots filled pretty quickly, from when my wife checked them to a half an hour later they were nearly booked a few hours out.  That's good for them!

I was surprised to see a smoker in the back of the restaurant with someone putting full racks of ribs on it.  It's definitely a legit smoker, they have the wood stacked nearby and the ribs from where I was standing looked to be St. Louis style ribs.  

The restaurant is nice inside.  It's clean, well laid out and has a good atmosphere.  We got a table on the patio which is fully enclosed and heated.  Due to covid, there were a lot of tables they weren't able to use, so we couldn't grab a seat by the bar (which I prefer).  

The staff were all very friendly and did a great job.  They definitely work as a team which makes our experience better.  

I grabbed a Yards in a can, but they do have a pretty impressive drink list.  This location is part of Boardroom Spirits so all of the alcohol was from BR.  

We came for the pizza, but their menu was more than just that.  I'm not quite sure how to categorize it...it's not a pizza place, it's not a bbq place, it's not a burger place or a salad place; but they offer all of that.

We ordered the Pulled Pork Nachos and the Detroit Style Pepperoni pizza.  The nachos were okay, they honestly would've been better without the pork.  The pork wasn't bad, it just didn't have flavor.  If something is called "smoked", I want to taste smoke and with their offset smoker setup they can definitely bring some flavor.  The cheese on the nachos was good as was the seasoning they put on their chips.  The toppings aside from the pork were good too.  I probably wouldn't order again if I returned.  

The pizza came out and looked great.  I have high expectations for what people call Detroit style...I'm from Detroit and have been eating this stuff before the "foodie" community was even born.  It looked good upon arrival, the cheese was crusted around the edge, the pepperoni had crisped up, the sauce was on top and there was grated parmesan (although more than I would usually expect.  And finally, there was a chiffonade of basil...something I wasn't excited about as I find it can be pretty over powering and if bruised during prep it's way too over powering. 

Took a bite and I was intrigued, the dough was crips along the outside but pillowy soft in the crumb.  The sauce was perfect, a little sweet but not much and it was room temp, not cold, not hot...perfect!  But then the basil, it was delicate, not over powering as I expected and the flavor of it is exactly what a pizza like this needs to cut through the richness of it.  

The pizza is small, only four pieces so if you're hungry or feeding a group get a few.  It's $14 which when you think about it, if you split it, you spent $7 on a very good lunch.  Plus the smaller size means there's less to take home.  

Overall I would definitely return to Northbound.  I want to try some of their cocktails, I want to try some of the other pizzas and some of their ribs.  I'm hoping the nachos were a one off.  But even if everything else on the menu was as underwhelming as the nachos...the pizza makes it worth the visit.

do they care about the conditions the puppies are born in and spend their formative weeks in? this is why puppy mill puppies bite and have separation anxiety and are notoriously difficult to house train and crate train. ...and those are the least of their problems. dogs are companion animals. in amish puppy mills they're viewed as a crop and the farmers cut as many corners as possible to turn as big a profit as possible. if you don't believe this, just do a very small amount of googling.

text:
This is my favorite in Delaware.  The menu is simple and perfectly executed.  Rolls are reasonably priced, artfully made and are PACKED with fish!  I do believe they use flash-frozen sashimi grade fish, but the color, texture, taste and smell are perfect.  Easily the best spicy tuna I have ever had.  I think the secret is the kewpie mayo along w/ the right amount of sriracha and sichimi powder.  Frankly, I can't get enough of this place and have at times, eaten it every day for lunch for weeks.  I've gone as far as to pick it up for dinner AFTER having had it for lunch. Their introduction of short-grain brown sushi rice has been great!

The Sushiman, YC Park is amazing to watch.  I've seen him skin a cucumber with a sword-like sushi knife in no time flat, in a single ribbon and then continue to shave it into a nori thin sheet for his tuna naruto roll roll.  The temaki are as big as a carnival iced cream cone.  You can barely finish one of them, there is so much fish in there.  The nigiri are beautiful.  Uniform pieces of fresh fish, perfectly perched on the best sushi rice I've ever had (just the right amount of vinegar and sugar).

Skip the newly opened Kooma.  Save Mikimotos for a night out, but go to Tokyo for lunch!  The owners are lovely, so support them in this tough economy.  If you must eat sushi, eat it here!

Why not 5 stars?  I have to save it for places that serve the local fresh fish, plucked out of the water that morning.  Let me know if you find a place that does!

text:
The customer service at this location is a real disappointment. 

We ordered contactless delivery for an order of 2 pizzas and a soda and when the delivery person left the order we discovered the soda had been forgotten.

We tried to call them but waited a total of more than 10 minutes on hold over the course of 2 calls (we got disconnected the first time having never spoken to anyone).

I then reached out via the contact form for our online order and the manager (Colby?) called us back and left a voicemail saying he could have the delivery driver bring the soda if we wanted and claiming the phone system was having issues but if I wanted to call back they had fixed it.

I returned his call after 25-30 minutes (we did not notice the voicemail right away) and got through. But he told me that the delivery driver had gone home (at 4pm on a Saturday?) and so they would place a credit on my account for the soda and I would get it with my next order. Though I agreed to this, as soon as I got off the phone I realized what a disappointing solution this was.

I ordered something, paid for it, tipped the delivery driver, and did not receive what I paid for. It was disappointing enough to not have the soda to go with the meal but then even the offer that it would be delivered that day was revoked and instead I was left in the position of having to place a future order in order to get something I had already paid for. 

The way the store offered to compensate for their mistake was to force me to order again to get what I paid for? This didn't seem right so I followed up with Dominoes customer care and explained all of the above.

The paraphrased response I got from Brenda H. was "We're chronically understaffed so mistakes happen. Sorry about the inconvenience. I have verified that there is a credit on your account for that soda."

After this disappointing response I figured I would simply ask for my money back and be done with it. When I responded, I told her I was not happy with that solution and would prefer not to loan Dominoes the $2.30 I paid for the soda until the next time I ordered (which was becoming increasingly unlikely based on this experience). I asked that they just refund the cost of the soda to the credit card I used to pay.

Brenda responded back telling me that I would have to call her and give my credit card information over the phone.

Yikes!

Forgetting the soda was a simple mistake that could have been no big deal. It would have been easily corrected with a refund or even just sending the driver immediately back out when they realized the issue (instead of waiting for me to confirm that I did in fact want the item I ordered for deliver, delivered). 

After sending the delivery driver home within a window of 30 minutes after offering to send him back out, and then putting me in a position where I had to place a future order to get something I already paid for, it would have been nice if they offered something as an apology. 
An order of cheese bread? A second soda? Really anything at all that says "Yeah, we messed this up. Here's something for the inconvenience."

But they did none of this. 
They messed up the order the first time.
Offered a solution and then rescinded it.
Settled on a bad solution.
And then most frustratingly responded badly to my response that I was disappointed by the experience.

If this is common for Dominoes, I'd encourage them to reevaluate their approach to customer service. This is a great example of what not to do.

I won't be calling them to give my credit card number over the phone. And I guess I'll have to find a new place nearby to order delivery. 

If you're looking to order chain pizza in this area, I encourage you to avoid this location. Maybe try the Papa Johns right around the corner.

text:
Lots of smoothie choices that will make you feel healthy AF.

I've recently gone on a total smoothie kick. I realized that the only way I'm going to consume vegetables is if it is in liquid form so I can inhale it quickly. Usually, I'll make a kale/spinach/banana/sunflower butter/chia seed/almond milk smoothie at home, but sometimes I get curious about what great flavor combinations exist outside my bubble. Enter Xtreme Juice. After reading a whole lot of reviews from Tampa Bay Yelpers I trust (thank you Elites!) I decided to make the foray into South Tampa to try this place.

After reading that the lines can get ridiculously long, I decided to go when I figured nobody would be there, at 10:30 a.m. on a Monday. Too late for breakfast, pretty early for lunch, I figured it was a safe bet. Well, there wasn't a line, but there was still a pretty steady stream of people. When I got there, there were three people waiting on their drink and while I waited for mine, four more people arrived. When you're serving what the people want, you don't get a downtime!

I'm so glad I looked at the menu (and read reviews) before I went. They have a massive menu! At first look, the size grabs your attention. Upon closer inspection, the drumsticks are large but it's the ton of breading that adds the girth and also makes it hard to fit in your mouth. Tried pulling apart with 2 forks but the meat did not fall off the bone easily like when I make chicken at home. After figuring out how to eat the drumstick and removing 1/2 the batter, the chicken was Ok. The flavor, of course, is in soaked into the breading. The Spicy was hot with a good wing burn. We determined the Wednesday "Wing" Special was fair at $5/lb but no way worth the usual $8.95. We did enjoy the Single Visit salad bar with real bacon bits even for the full price of $5.95 as the "wings" are not considered an entrée rating the $3.95 price. Out third trip total and second for "Wing" Wednesday was not as exciting as the first. 3lbs of "wings" arrived, were even bigger than before with even more batter. The size made it almost impossible to fit in your mouth and the batter would fall off, causing the "wing" to fall to the basket. The three of us gave up and used forks and knives to get through the meal. Same as before, the meat did not want to come off the bone and with 4 of the 5 "wings" finished, I threw in the towel. The flavor is fine, I like the spice but the batter and chicken meat was not great.

text:
Like the other *very few* non 5-star reviews, I feel that I must lead with a preface. I do not discredit any awards this restaurant has won or knock Chef Shaya for any reason. However, if I force myself to be completely objective, I believe 4 stars is an accurate reflection of my dining experience. 

My husband made a reservation 2 months ago for a Saturday night dinner and the day finally came for us to dine here! I would say reservations are totally necessary here unless you are fine with bar seating (which to me seemed crowded) but I was also informed there is a courtyard open on good weather days that does not require reservations (didn't see this space for myself). 

A quick glance around the restaurant revealed a full house filled with parties of all sizes, no kids/teens, and glasses of wine on almost every table. It's a very 'sexy restaurant'--dark, beautiful lighting, upbeat music, and plates intended to be shared...a tad on the loud side. Our server stopped by promptly asking if we had any questions about the menu and to take our drink orders. We ordered the lamb kebab from the small plates section, three selections from the 'for the table' section (3 for $15 special), and the cauliflower hummus. 

The plates arrived in shifts which was fine but the lamb kebab was seriously delayed--I politely reminded our server that we had ordered the lamb since we had finished our other plates and she said that the dishes come out in courses. It just seemed odd that something from the small plates (which I took to mean appetizers) would come out last. But as far as the taste, the lamb was tender and flavorful similar to lamb at other Mediterranean places. You get two "links" of lamb in the order. 

For the 3 for $15 dishes, we chose the shipka peppers, the baba ghanoush, and the Israeli salad. I was disappointed in the shipka peppers as they were essentially bell papers filled with goat cheese; I love goat cheese but was just now wowed by the dish. You get two peppers in the order. The baba ghanoush and Israeli salad were tasty, also similar to other Mediterranean restaurants in the city.

The cauliflower hummus was very good but I must point out that it is not hummus made out of cauliflower (don't know if that is obvious or not). Instead, it is nicely seasoned and spiced cauliflower atop hummus. The best comparison I can make is that the cauliflower was very similar to Indian aloo gobi. Very tasty and my second favorite selection of the evening.

My most favorite thing you ask? The pita! Seriously, the pita is as fluffy as a pillow! So warm, delicious, chewy, carb-y, just perfection. The servers bring you a pita at a time and eating with your hands is totally allowed (err..we did at least). There was a point in the evening where we were pita-less for almost 10 minutes before someone brought us another one. Diners definitely need constant pita supply for all of the hummus-trimmed dishes!

We enjoyed the food and will definitely come back. I just think I got bit by the very high expectation bug on this one!

I can say that it is a bit pricey. Dinner usually rounds out to about 80-100 dollars for the two of us but it's honestly VERY very well deserved. Excellent customer service, and excellent food. Will always be our favorite and our cherished tradition.

I hope Nan never renovates its outside decor because too many people would storm our hidden gem.

text:
This is really a tragedy.  I'll start with problems.

First, the place is badly laid out, with cramped seating and weird dividers leading you to believe the designer was being purposefully obtuse.  It's two levels, but you have to go outside to get to the second level.  They don't have enough tables or bar space; good luck fighting your way through to get a beer.

Second, they were utterly slammed when I went, and that's apparently not unusual.  This would be merely an inconvenience, except that it's amplified by the cramped conditions and the ridiculous layout.  It's made worse when their hostess can't seem to figure out who's on the list and seats a party of two at a four top when a two top is open and six or seven parties of four are waiting.  She sent us upstairs on our own to sit at the worst table in the house. ("It's the one next to the shuffleboard," she said).

Third, it's unbelievably loud.  Concert front row loud.  Raucous shuffleboarder loud.  Meal-ruining loud.  Unless you're deaf, the upstairs will be seriously unpleasant.

Fourth, and perhaps unpardonably, the beer is just bizarre.  I've sampled lots of beer brewed by brewers big, small and backyard, and this stuff is weird.  I understand Belgian brewers do odd things, it's why I love Belgian beers.  But these brewers are doing something truly strange, producing bodiless, watery beers completely dominated by sour flavors.  The black was sort of like a bitter lemonade, the white a sea of strange esters, and the triple mixing the two.

Fifth, the staff cannot, really cannot, cope.  Some are trying, some are wandering in a shell-shocked daze.  There is no one in overall command and no sign of a motivating intelligence or overarching goal.  I suspect the management escaped from some kind of group home for felonious MBA types, and has decided to use their brilliance to pilot a restaurant straight into the ground.

These would just be the typical problems for a hot restaurant in fashionable neighborhood, things to cluck about before it goes the way of tapas joints to make room for the next trend.  But the food is really good.  It's tasty and well-conceived.  The fries are terrific.  The sandwiches are large and filling, their meats savory and delicious.  The sausage board does not impress.  The herring salad, while delicious, is bizarrely presented unmixed and unmixable within the confines of its bowl, and surrounded by ice-bound olives (pits intact) and chunks of gherkin.  The crepes are competent.  It's good food.  Without the unweatherable storm of noise, crowding, short service and weird beer, this would be a really great place.  But I doubt that whoever is in charge has the will, or the self-critical capacity, to make that happen.

The staff is amazing here. Probably some of the best service in Edmonton, hard to come by, even when they are busy.

text:
For my inaugural visit to NOLA, it sure was nice to end our two week Caribbean vacation at The Ritz Carlton New Orleans. 

LOCATION:
The utmost convenience as they're on Canal Street just one block from the start of Bourbon Street's busy stretch.  There are tons of restaurants and shops nearby within walking distance. 

ATMOSPHERE:
It's your typical marble-laden Ritz Carlton.  The main lobby and registration desk are on the second floor, forcing you to use the elevators twice in order to access your room.  A beautiful courtyard sits off the lobby & lounge that's decorated with beautiful foliage surrounded by the hotel on all four sides. 

ROOM:
We overlooked the center courtyard with a sliver view of the mighty Mississippi, though there are no balconies here.  Decor was very inviting with warm colors, rich designs and exquisite fabrics.  Sleep quality was good with a strong a/c, comfortable bed & pillows, quiet rooms and all the usual amenities.  The ice machine is near the elevators.  Oddly you still pay for Wi-Fi here and charging ports were lacking. 

BATHROOM:
Single basin, shower-tub combo and enclosed lavatory.  Water pressure was strong with fast drainage.  The amenities are very perfume-y but luckily my home-brought stash was still full so no problems here. 

DAVENPORT LOUNGE:
We retired one evening to the jazz sounds of Jeremy Davenport, the headliner the lounge is named after.  Drinks were pricey but this is The Ritz.  The lounge also hosts twice daily tea service. 

SERVICE:
The only staff I interacted with were two friendly housekeepers that were tending to our room as we returned at an odd time.  I'm sure we were a breath of fresh air for them from the usual stuffy guests they have to deal with.  

TIPS:
Be sure to try the complimentary gumbo cart stationed across the front desk in the afternoon time.  The gumbo was amazingly delish but sadly ruined all other gumbo experiences for me in the city.  A take home copy of the recipe is located in the room, but I have yet to attempt it.  

There is a short cut to Bourbon Street without having to use the main entrance on Canal Street.  From the lobby, walk through the Davenport Lounge and take the elevators to the first level.  You'll end up near the meeting rooms which lets you out on the corner of Dauphine & Iberville.  Coming back in requires key access. 

OVERALL:
There isn't anything as rewarding as coming back to a high end hotel after a long, hot, humid, sticky day in the Big Easy.

I told James that we were interested in this particular car, he asked me to hold on and checked on the car. He then said the car was still there. I asked him how I would go about finding out the details of what would be involved in purchasing this car since I lived almost 300 miles away and wanted to make sure everything would work before travelling that far. He directed me to fill out the application online and said he would call me back once he got it.

Not too long later, he called me back and told me that I would qualify for the car. I then asked for details and explained to him what I in order to purchase the car. I also stated that I wanted payments no more that $400 a month and an interest rate no higher than 10% and preferred lower than that. James again said he would check on things and give me a call back. 

He called me back and stated that there should be no problem meeting everything I wanted. I was told my payment would be under $400 a month and should have an interest rate of around 8% with nothing down and based on my trade in being in good condition (more on that later).

I got the car ready and called James again to inform that we would be on the way, he said great everything would be ready when I got there. Half way there, he even called to get some more needed information.

Too be honest, I couldn't believe another burger restaurant was opening in Carrollwood. I mean really, we already have Burger Monger, Burger 21 and Five Guys just across the street! But curiosity took the better of my wife and me and we went to see the latest in carnivorous fare. 
     Upon entering, if you don't like the 80's, you are already in trouble. Posters adorn the walls and 80's music is blaring from the speakers. It is a fun vibe, but I forgot my Miami Vice pastels at the cleaners. 
     The menu is very simple...Burgers, fries, onion rings, shakes and beverages. The staff was very friendly and informative with us "newbies." My wife and I stayed with the basics of cheeseburgers, a side of fries (they only come in one size) and sodas from the soda fountain of  the future machine. I had to say I was a little taken aback that for just that order it was $25.00. If we wanted two shakes it would have been an additional $10. 
      We sat down to wait for our order in the dining area that seats about fifty maybe less on retro chairs and tables. There is also a HDTV on the wall. When the the food arrived if came on huge pizza style metal pates that were way over-sized for our burgers and there was a separate plate for the fries. They made the table a little crowded. 
     Now, down to the taste. The burgers were good solid burgers.  I had mine all-the-way including caramelized onions, pickle lettuce and Mojo sauce. It had charcoal flavor to it and was made to order. My wife's burger was with just the cheese and she added her ketchup table-side.  The fries, we ordered extra crispy and they too came out as ordered. They were very good and my only distraction was that the one size was more than just the two of us could finish, it would have been nice to have a smaller amount as to not waste them.
     Overall, it was an okay meal. As my rating suggests, "I've had better." And that is probably not the rating you want with so many other burger places just literally seconds away.

Had a quick lunch here with my parents who happened to be vacationing with us in Tampa this week.  We checked this place out since it was close to their hotel.  It was 1130 am on a wednesday so there weren't a lot of places open for business yet.

We were seated momentarily after walking in, and were served by a gentleman who looked like he was in training.  He spoke rather quietly, and even though we were only one table of 5 that were seated, he found it hard to either speak up or loosen up.  I hope he gets better since he would have a hard time during busy hours with a fair amount of humdrum.

The Thai thani stuffed chicken wings looked really good so we had an order of that along with the traditional summer rolls as appetizers.  They had no Thai iced coffee to my dismay, so I had the regular hot coffee.  Everyone else had iced water on this hot Tampa noon.

After placing an order for lunch servings of Pad Thai, chicken and mushrooms and rice, and sour seafood soup (my parents wanted to try it), we received a complimentary helping of salad.  It was a bit weird because it was the same cheap salad you normally get at a sushi joint; cheap iceberg lettuce and lifeless shredded carrots with a slathering of what looked to be Ginger-carrot-citrus dressing.  I didn't eat mine, since it didn't look as appetizing as I was hoping it would be.  Besides, I'm not a salad guy.  I waited patiently.

The stuffed wings arrived shortly and they were perfectly crisp on the outside.  The stuffing inside consisted of mushrooms, vermicelli and chicken meat in a nice flavored combo.

I tried the pad Thai next.  I'm no expert at pad thai but the noodles looked like they were soaked in dark soy sauce.  I say soaked because the noodles didn't have the "spring" of freshly cooked noodles.  The noodles were either cooked too long or was cooked with too much liquid.  The taste was rather bland, it didn't have the balance of other pad Thai dishes I've had (needed more tart- vinegar or tamarind perhaps?). I also noticed the lack of paprika and eggs in the dish.  I may sound hypercritical but my girl is Thai, so my expectations are pretty high especially when her grandmother makes delicious home dishes.

I moved on to the chicken and mushrooms dish, but it reminded me of Chinese food- I had some jasmine rice with it.  It was just ok, it had no character to it and I can't remember for the life of me what the rest of the ingredients were.


Bottom line-  I was expecting better execution to their dishes to match their interior decor.  I believe that a place needs to match their decor with their service.  When I walked in, I felt good, my eyes liked what they saw; but even though  I did leave full, my experience was not  satiated- a bit dissapointing considering the cruise ships unload nearby.

I still give it an "ok" 3 since I don't think it's fair to compare commercial food to a home cooked meal, and the server was being trained, so service suffered a bit...... He needs to train on someone sometime, and that was us.

THE DUCK.

The group consensus was also that he was hilarious, and we enjoyed our spots of light banter even on a very busy night.

Four stars instead of five? I had tried to call ahead to let them know we would arrive with a larger group and never heard back. text:
My husband loves hibachi, so every so often, I humor him and take him to a hibachi grill.  Personally, I think hibachi is mediocre food whose popularity depends on an audience that likes to watch someone twirl a spatula and flip shrimp.

We showed up and were asked to wait at the bar until another party showed up wanting hibachi.  We sat for about 10 minutes before getting seated.  Luckily, we were able to take advantage of the Happy Hour at the bar, and two generous pours of wine was less than $11.

Hibachi at Oishi includes the main protein but also fried rice, fried noodles, miso soup, salad and mixed vegetables.  That's a ridiculous amount of food.  Of course, it's not "cheap," especially since I could make the same meal for less money at home (and probably make it taste better with less fat too!).  Whatever.  At least I don't have to do the food prep and clean up afterwards.  

Our chef wasn't Japanese, but outside of a few cities, most hibachi chefs aren't.  He was very nice, and he was pretty good at flipping things into his hat or front pocket.  

I had the tenderloin and scallops.  My husband had the tenderloin and shrimp.  Everything was cooked as ordered, and I haven't had such tender scallops in a long time.  The side stuff was fine.  The miso soup was unremarkable but inoffensive.  I wasn't crazy about the salad dressing.  I didn't really see the point to having both fried rice and fried noodles, but whatever.  The dipping sauces were completely unnecessary, unless you love salt and more salt with a side of sugar on already-seasoned meat.

All in all, it was a perfectly adequate meal, but nothing wowed me (although hibachi pretty much never wows me).  I wouldn't mind coming back the next time my husband wants hibachi, but maybe I'll try their sushi next time instead.

I'm beginning to have my doubts about food trucks in general here in Nashville. Believe me, I love the idea. However, nearly every one I've patronized has been over priced, you wait forever for the food and when you finally get your food it's kinda mediocre. Such was the case yesterday with Riff's at Centennial Park. We got to the park later in the day. The only thing on the menu was burritos and tacos. Reading other reviews, I know you do others things besides tacos. I went for the fish tacos. I didn't want the pineapple salsa so I asked if they had any hot sauce. Puzzled at my request, the woman who took my order said they could put jerk sauce on the fish, which sounded great to me. So seven bucks for two tacos. During the nearly 30 minute wait I watched burritos being made. I saw plentiful helpings of chicken and brisket, rice and beans (mostly rice), gobs of pineapple salsa and some type of greens going into the burritos. At this point I'm thinking wow, if the burritos look as good, my taco should be great. Again, almost 30 minutes later, which is WAY TOO LONG to wait, my name is called and the guy hands me my tacos and says, ''Sorry for the wait (which was the standard line for everyone when they came up for their food). I made three orders of these before I remembered not to put the pineapple salsa on it". I said, "no problem' but, what I really meant was, 'what the hell took so long, it's just a couple of tacos?". I start to walk away and look down at what I just waited a half and hour and seven buck for and it's just tortillas and two pieces of fish with this sweet jerk sauce on it. That's it! No garnishment what so ever! No slice of lime. Nothing! Seven bucks and a half hour of standing around in the hot sun for this?!? No, I didn't go back and complain. I was tired of waiting as were my wife and kids.

C'mon, Riff's! You want to know how to make great tacos? Quit with the gourmet angle and go visit some taco trucks on Nolensville or Murfreesboro Roads. It's quite simple. You take two small corm tortillas, put a couple choices of meat on it, then cilantro and onions, a couple slices of lime and your done. Offer some hot sauce at the point the customer picks up the order. The same advice goes for Mas Taco. Quit trying to re-invent the taco. Oh, and charge half the price. text:
Bourbon Street and the Bayou with a Brooklyn sensibility

If this place isn't a local landmark, it should be. Galliano brings the bistro treatment to the indigenous cuisine of Louisiana. 

From an outsider perspective, it is admittedly hard to know what constitutes authentic Louisiana cuisine, but I know delicious food and this place most certainly has it. 

The gumbo, to me, is the standout. It comes boiling hot in a little cauldron that would singe the hairs on your arm if it got too close. Also noteworthy are the duck wings -- succulent and tender with a sauce that curious mix of Tobasco and some sort of Szechuan flavor. The stuffed pork chop that I coveted and stole from my friend's plate had the smokiness of good BBQ brisket but without the fattiness. The Sunday pot roast was completely unexpected. Being a Bostonian, I have a preconceived notion of what a pot roast is -- you know, the "Yankee" kind. This was an unexpected riff on the classic with dirty rice, something called "poor man's gravy" that was plenty rich for me, and bits of what I think were sweet potatoes. It was tender and delicious. The desserts are worth saving room for, I recommend either the Cherries Jubilee (yay, fire!) or the peanut butter cup cake. 

Galliano represents New Orleans' culinary reputation well, such that after a disappointing venture to an actual "landmark restaurant" that was so abysmal I couldn't even eat it (but that is another review),  we went back to Galliano because we knew we would leave full and happy.

Service needs to be worked on. Dishes I liked -

- Veal Sinatra
- Veal Parmesan

text:
Ok here goes. I'm 60 years old and have never had a tattoo, but that doesn't mean I haven't wanted one. For several years I have talked about getting a tattoo of a very famous fairy (why? I'm not sure.  Probably has something to do with my dysfunctional upbringing, or just crazy about the Mouse.). I finally had a few extra bucks in my pocket and thought I would finally take the plunge. Why Skinquake?  I've had opportunities in other towns and in other states, but I finally chose Skinquake. They were not in a bad location, they are in a very nice strip mall. They did not have tinted, or no, windows, they are wide open. And they had an artist named Kari (my first name, just spelled differently). So I walk in, not accosted by blaring music (also not classical, that would be too strange). Not overwhelmed by drawings of skulls and crossbones (yes there are drawings on the wall, duh!). But a very good, efficient tattoo shop. They greet me (sure the guys there have tattoos, it is a tattoo parlor after all), and when I tell them what I want they don't blink an eye and they don't comment, they quote me a price, I accept and make an appointment for the next day. 
Next day, I'm a bit nervous when my appointment time comes. I meet Kari, show her a photo of what I want, tell her where I want it and she takes my photo goes to a machine, where the magic begins, makes a stencil and it begins. I'm shaved, the stencil is applied and I'm settled into a chair (it's sort of like a barber shop with the open windows and the chairs, nothing hidden). Then the point of no return, I suppose I could have just stopped when I first felt the needle hit the skin and just had another freckle on my leg, but it was not as bad as I had anticipated, more annoying. They patter of conversations between the two Karis (Carey) was also very reminiscent of a barber shop, do you have any children? How long have you lived here? And does you wife know you're getting a tattoo (oh at this point I should point out that, even at 60, they wanted to see my driver's license, which I thought was very professional). Kari was very efficient, explaining to me the process as she applied the ink, and even accommodated me when I wanted to send a photo of the process to my wife. I felt the whole process was handled in a very professional manner, very courteous, and very efficient. 
Within about an hour, my very famous fairy was completed, I was given after care instructions and she looked wonderful. I paid,I tipped (very important) and I walked out a very happy customer. Will I go to them again? Not very likely (I probably will never get another tattoo). Will I recommend Skinquake?  I think by now, dear reader, you have that answer.  Being a tech savvy 60 year old I couldn't wait to get home to post this on Facebook, but first I had to show it to my wife (who helped me find the right pixie pose), and I had to tell the kids and Grandkids. Did it make it to Facebook?  Oh yeah!  It is as indelibly posted on the internet just as it is on my skin.

text:
I came with my Ramen Club to experience what Let's Grill had to offer. It was a slow Saturday afternoon during a rather cold February. We were seated in the centre of the restaurant at a long, rectangular table with seating for 10. I think we all looked forward to a hot bowl of comforting ramen to pick up our spirits. 

When I checked in on Yelp, I was surprised to find that Let's Grill has a deal! Excitedly, I ordered the tako yaki and explored the menu further. They have a number of appetizers on offer such as house salad, seaweed salad and chicken karrage. Not sure if the menu that day was their standard one or a simplified lunch version. Either way, it had ramen so we were set. 

You can choose between four different variations on their pork soup stock: shoyu, miso, spicy and black garlic ramen. Each bowl comes with the same garnishes which included 2 soft boiled eggs, 2 slices of pork, corn, green onions, dried seaweed, and lotus root chips. I ordered the black garlic which was probably the most popular order at our table. 

The ramen was served as it was ready which meant two to three people received their soup at a time. The kitchen only had one cook while the front of the house had only one server. This limited service to a large group like ours. When the bowls arrived, they looked good and I found the garlic oil in mine smelled great. Upon first taste, the broth was good but that is about as good as it got. The noodles were far too overdone which was a common complaint from others at the table. The egg was non-marinated, which is fine but not what many of us where used to. I realize it says soft boiled egg on the menu but it isn't what people were used to. It was so soft that it broke apart when touched and simply lacked the flavour a marinated egg can add. The other ingredients were the standard, safe ones you would expect in a ramen. Add all together, it meant overall the bowl was underwhelming. I wasn't disappointed but others certainly were.

If someone said they wanted to go here for lunch I think I would come again. The tako yaki was good and I don't mind a ramen that plays it safe. However, if you want to experience the best ramens Edmonton has to offer, we would be going elsewhere.

text:
Verde's was a totally delicious surprise! I wanted Mexican food after my doctor's appointment and remembered this fairly new restaurant on Main Street.

Street parking is available on Main Street and marked lot parking is located behind the restaurant with a walk thru archway. I was told valet parking is an option in the evening.

The upscale restaurant is warm, cozy and attractive with dark wood tables, booths, bar and tall top tables. Patio seating is located in front of the restaurant along Main Street weather permitting. 

The weekday specials are great! Monday kid's eat free and 1/2 price cocktails, Tuesday and Thursday house margaritas are 1/2 price at $6 and Wednesday is $2 tacos. 

Verde's serves affordable lunches on Monday thru Friday from 11:00 - 3:00 ranging from $9 - $13. There's lunch combos of choose two choices from enchilda, taco, burrito, tamale, quesadilla or tostada served with rice and beans for $8 and there's two street tacos served with one side from $7-$11 and daily $9 specials. The lunch menu also features various types of tacos, fajitas, torta, grilled chicken (arroz con pollo) enchiladas, chimichanga, taco salad, burrito or chilaquiles con carne. 

I only tried a couple chips in the medium salsa and both were perfectly acceptable. I ordered the Enchiladas Mole with chicken in corn tortillas smothered in house made mole sauce. Their mole sauce is now one of my all time favorites. The spices are well balanced and not overly sweet. If you enjoy mole sauce I highly recommend you try. I subbed the refried beans for the rice and they were creamy and not greasy like so many refried beans. For dessert I ordered the Tres Leches Cake to go. The cake was sweet and moist, made with 3 types of milk and topped with drunken berries. Scrumptious dessert and it traveled well.

My server was excellent, attentive, informative and personable. 

I certainly will be scheduling another visit to Verdes soon. Verdes has a sister restaurant in Avon I need to visit too.

Friends and fellow Yelpers Rick and Holly Garrett are regulars at Big Mike's Cafe, partly owing to the fact that Big Mike's hosts an acoustic jam every other Monday night that they put together but also because it's close to their home and a mighty fine place for a meal. 

While I've not yet made it over for Monday nights, I finally found myself in the neighborhood on a Friday after work and decided it would be a great time to try it out. 

I arrived at Big Mike's early in the dinner hour and, in fact, was the only customer when I arrived. That didn't last for long. I was greeted with a warm enthusiasm by Katie and, not surprisingly, offered my table of choice. Big Mike's is located in a small strip center next to a liquor store and in a building with a Chinese restaurant, a video retailer of some sort, and a brand new cupcake shop. Being at 96th & College, it's right on the line between Carmel and Indy and surrounded by offices. I will admit that I was mighty tempted by their pizzas, which happened to be on special tonight, but looking at the sizes concluded there was no way I could down one on my own and I really wasn't looking to take anything home. I considered their tenderloin, which Rick G. really likes, but decided to keep it simple and go for their 1/2 pound burger with cheese along with a side of your choice (I chose fries, but could have gone for slaw, chips, cottage cheese, or potato salad). The meal was $10 and it was another $1.95 for my usual unsweetened iced tea. 

The dining room is pretty simple, a nice Americana decor with oldies music (like Simon & Garfunkel) playing overhead. While it's easy to get used to the distractions that many restaurants put out there, it's kind of nice to have a restaurant you can go to and actually have a conversation. They offer a variety of other appetizers, sandwiches, and a couple of meal options. I've heard their desserts are killer, but I opted out this time around. 

The sign "Let our family, serve your family" gives you an idea of what to expect from Big Mike's, a place that also offers catering for private parties. You're going to be welcomed, remembered, and appreciated here. If they make a mistake, they're going to immediately own it and fix it (as I saw happen tonight). In short, this was a place I just plain enjoyed hanging out. 

The burger was served on a buttered pretzel bun, an interesting choice that added a distinct flavor to the beef. I won't say it's my favorite burger, but I enjoyed it and would have no problem recommending it. The fries complemented the burger well, lightly browned and having a simple yet agreeable texture. The unsweetened iced tea was terrific and served in a rather nicely sized mason jar, a jar that was so big I didn't even need my usual refill. 

When I return, and I'm pretty comfortable saying when, I find myself really wanting to try their pizza. It looks terrific. I also think this is a place I would enjoy on those nights I simply want to read and on those nights when I want to meet a friend for dinner. It has a casual, comfortable feeling to it. 

My meal came in at right about $13 plus tip. The serving sizes were good, the customer service was great, and it was an awesome way to close out a busy week. 

Big Mike's is a true family business. Katie and Mike are brother/sister, Katie specializing in the front-end and Mike being the kitchen wizard. They even feature desserts from their mother, whose desserts were popular at The Abbey (Man, I miss that place!). 

So, if you're keeping score. Good food. Great service. Local. They host local musicians. 

They're freaking awesome.

text:
I have mixed feelings about this hotel.

My stay here was for about a week and I had a decent deal through Priceline for about $50 per night.  I guess because of the deal I got, I was treated like an ugly, red-headed stepchild -- they put me all the way to the right and in the back with the lovely airport parking lot as my view.  When I went back to see if I could change it, they told me that all the rooms were booked.  I counted 20 cars in the lot that night.  It was highly unlikely I was told the truth.

They contract out this hotel to some airlines and to the FedEx trucking company, so you'll see a bunch of FedEx trucks parked on the right, backside of the parking lot.  They were my neighbors for the extend of my stay.  They check-in during the day and check-out at night.  I must say that truckers made great neighbors; never heard a peep from them.  I guess driving 8-10 hours a day can wear a guy down.  So if you're staying in the rear of the hotel, please be respectful to those truckers (they sleep during the day).


The hotel is decent.  Clean, firm beds, friendly staff, and two workstations by the check-in area for public use (complementary printing).  Free ice water with a dash of lemon by the stations.

I didn't bother to try much of the other facilities.  My time was spend mostly outdoors.  If you haven't been to Tucson before, you should really visit the national parks here.  They are quite beautiful.  (Not during the summer, of course)

My picks:

Sabino Canyon - my fav

Sanguaro National park - gates pass area is nice

Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum - a must for kids, make this your first stop to learn about the environment.

Mt. Lemmon - beautiful drive.  Snow during winter.

Extra time to kill:

Picacho Peak (hike it if you're in decent shape, the site where the only Civil War battle in Arizona was fought) (closed during summer, 'cause they don't want you to die from heat stroke (my guess)).

San Xavier del Bac Mission (white church painted by 3rd rate artists, skip if you're not into religion.)


In short, if you book through an online company, you will most likely be treated like an ugly red-headed stepchild and be sent to the worst rooms in the hotel.  If you don't have a car, you may be stuck eating in the hotel restaurant.  I heard from others that it was actually pretty good.  I didn't take the chance.  There are a few fast food (Burger King, Subway) joints a few blocks away (5-10 minutes walk).  Free airport shuttle.  I didn't hear any commercial planes, but I heard a few jet fighters flying around.  They were loud, but only during the day and didn't occur often.


I will probably not return.  Didn't like the way I was treated.

text:
I had never stayed in a Drury Inn prior to this trip.  We headed to STL for my brothers wedding and booked a room where they had reserved a room block.  It was a great location, the rooms were clean and reasonably comfortable and the staff was nice.  The breakfast was ample and the only thing I was really missing was a mixed fruit bowl... though they did have bananas or apples.    

One night there was an incident with a fire alarm at 2:00am, where the guests all had to go into the parking lot to wait while fire trucks came and then left without passing along much, if any, information to the bedraggled bunch in the parking lot.  While I completely respect that the hotel had no control over the fire alarm, a bit more information would have been greatly appreciated!  After all your guests were awakened in the middle of the night, ran outside with little to no belongings (in one case a father came out with his wife and two kids wearing just his boxers!  I totally applaud that guy for responding the way we all should, though I did take time to throw on some clothes), waited outside for about 30 minutes and then were told we could reenter.  Upon reentering, we found that the alarms were still going off in all the rooms, so we camped in the hallway for an additional 20 minutes or so.  

However, I feel the collective questions the guests had were, "Why did the fire alarm go off?  Was there a fire?!? Will breakfast be extended the following morning, since we all got a less that ideal night sleep?  Will there be a credit for the inconvenience?"   All of my questions were answered the next morning after talking with the GM at breakfast.  There was a faulty pull station in the restaurant that set the alarm off.  They did take my suggestion and extended breakfast 1/2 hour and we were given a one night credit (though you had to ask for that).  With that being said, the hotel responded to a bizarre situation well, after the fact.  However, it would have been great to have more information provided without asking and while the incident was occurring.  

Over all it is not a Sheraton, but I really liked the Drury for what it was!

text:
After an especially hot and steamy viewing of Showgirls and a quick flip through the spring Victoria's Secret catalogue, I was in the mood for more cheap thrills. My pulse racing like I just got out of spin class, I arrived at Hooters on a Saturday like so many others, ready to take in the view, devour some delicious wings, and try not to embarrass myself while being chatted up by a college girl in a white and orange Halloween costume.

To my delight, it was Wrestling Day, and all of the waitresses were dressed as professional wrestlers. Appropriate, as my hung over waitress would have been better cast as The Undertaker. As I would soon find out, the "viewing" beats the chewing.

I ordered the all-you-can-eat boneless wings. As my dedicated readers know, I have a debilitating fear of birds, and believe touching their bones allows the bird's soul to torment me in the afterlife, so I generally stick to boneless wings. There I was, lounging sideways in my booth with my legs crossed, taking my first bite of a buffalo wing through my Mexican wrestler facemask with a manic look in my eyes, content with all in the world and expecting nothing but the best from the chefs at Hooters. What the sauce lacked for in quality it made up for in butter. However, the meat itself was like a dry piece of roadkill cartilage sprayed with the foam they use to seal cracks in your basement walls. And I know, having eaten my share of roadkill in my many trips to Nigeria to complete business deals with dying diamond mine heiresses.

I asked for more wings after dumping the remaining 9 1/2 wings on my plate on the floor under my table, and elected to go with the teriyaki wings. While chatting me up during a particularly long refill of my diet Dr. Pepper, my waitress asked me about my cell phone cover and asked if she could show the other waitresses. I didn't understand all the fuss about my custom self-portrait on the phone cover, but I figured it was harmless to let them admire it. Upon checking my phone later in the day, I noticed someone called Puerto Rico 11 times!

After a few minutes, my teriyaki wings came out. They had a corporate tang, a hint of mild depression - a charity-dinner appetizer made for 200 people in a sleezy Bangkok convention center. Needless to say, I dumped those as well, this time using my foot to discreetly push the growing graveyard of wasted chicken lives further under the table while coughing and waving at the hostess standing by the door to cover my movements.

I decided to take my final order to go, and because they apparently don't allow that on the all-you-can-eat option, I was forced to stick all 5 parmesan garlic wings in the pocket of my slacks.

I give 1 star for the wrestling promotion and the lovely Mexican wrestling mask (I plan to wear it often at home), and 1 additional star because I caught a 4 pound large-mouthed bass the next day when I used the parmesan garlic wings as bait. Delightfully "Tackley", Yet Unrefined indeed! I'll be sending them the dry-cleaning bill for my slacks. Be warned, vampire pick-pockets - the stench of garlic in my pockets is strong enough to kill.

I whipped out my phone and saw that my checking account balance was $42. Low, but last time I checked, $42 covers a $12 tab. In fact, it would cover a $12 tab with a 20% tip. And don't lecture me about spending 28% of my balance on alcohol. Payday is around the corner.

Back to the story...

I said that it must be an error, that I have adequate funds in my account, and to run the card again. Declined again. The waitress rudely barked that there better be somebody who can pay for me. A friend stepped up and graciously paid, but I was confused. 

This morning I called my bank and asked what was up. Turns out my card wasn't declined for $12, but for a $50 preauthorization that HOB runs on all open bar tabs. After a little research, I've found that this isn't an uncommon practice. While I don't like it, I can live with it. What I find to be unacceptable is that the cocktail waitress either didn't understand the preauthorization process or was simply unwilling to explain what was going on to me. Additionally, there was no signage warning patrons of the preauthorization.

Lesson learned: don't open a tab at HOB if you have less than $50 in your checking account.

text:
My husband and I made reservations at Sidney Street Cafe to celebrate Valentine's Day. We had never been before, but it seems like such a significant "player" in the St. Louis food scene and so well-recommended that it was time to give it a try.

When we arrived at the restaurant, it looked a bit dark at the bar, but as we walked toward the hostess, we saw inside the dining area that it was warmer and brighter. The hostess led us away from that dining area, down a hallway toward another room. I felt like I had left one restaurant and been taken to another that could aptly be named "The Dungeon." The room had skylights (it was after 5:30 in the winter, so no light to speak of there) hanging lights, there was a tiny candle on the table, but it really was just so dim that I felt myself leaning in to see the person across the table from me. We were told it was romantic, but this restaurant's "back room" is on the wrong side of the line between romantic and a creepy cellar.

The hostess set down a wine list and a small board containing a list of appetizers. We wondered what the list of main courses was so we could decide between them and the chef's tasting menu. Our waiter arrived and was not rude, but set the tone of painful pretentiousness for the rest of our visit - every ingredient of every dish was described in minute detail. I think restaurants believe this is part of the "theater of the experience," but it's just too much. That's not to say that the food did not warrant additional explanation, but people cannot process and retain a description of every ingredient that goes into every entree, appetizer, and dessert. After a lengthy description of two of the appetizers (there were about 10 on the board), I tuned the waiter out and just let him finish. At the end, he did mention that the chef's tasting menu was an option and contained five courses, including an amuse-bouche. I think that it is incorrect to advertise an amuse-bouche as a course. Amuse-bouche should be a "gift" from the chef to give them a glimpse of what is to come.

We were given time to consider the options, still without a dinner menu. When the waiter returned, he handed us the dinner menu and asked if we would like to order an appetizer. We should have gotten the dinner menu in advance in order to have time to decide between the listed options and the tasting menu, but we were committed to getting the artisan cheeses and the house-made charcuterie so we did not go the route of the tasting menu. The items were surprisingly scant. There were 16 pieces of meat arranged in rows of 4 on the charcuterie board. Other than the half-rounds of head cheese, the slices were shaved incredibly thinly and were tiny. I would rather have paid a little more to get something of more substance. The flavors of both plates were just ok. Between the two, the best part was the small pretzel rolls that arrived with the charcuterie board, which were chewy, fresh, and flavorful.

Again for the dinner course, we listened to the litany of preparations and ingredients that went into every dish. It was especially difficult to follow for the items that were off the menu. At one point, I heard the waiter talking about taking a blood orange, freezing it, shattering it, and then sprinkling the frozen shards over one of the dishes. That just seems like a lot of work to have something 'different' to tell diners. I did end up ordering the pork belly and my husband ordered the steak Au Poivre. I felt like my pork belly meal was well-prepared and tasty; I would not order it again because for my taste it became too rich, but that is my preference rather than a failing of the restaurant. My husband ordered his steak medium-rare. If a restaurant chooses to give a diner only a portion of a full strip steak and cut it for them, then they should be highly aware of the doneness of the meat they are serving. The steak my husband was served was definitely medium. It was served on top of what was essentially a fried mashed potato cake, which was delectable.

We did not try dessert as we had other plans, which was somewhat relieving to me as I didn't think that I could follow another at-length description. This restaurant has potential, but there is work to be done in finding balance. Preparation and ingredients are important, but if the food is good enough, it can speak for itself without making the diner tired and confused at the ordering stage. Whatever is being done to create a warm atmosphere in the front needs to be transitioned to the uninviting back. The waiter having a loud "look at me" conversation about "the foie I had in LA" needs to take it down a notch. I likely won't go here again; it's worth going once to make up your own mind, but I would strongly encourage you to visit other restaurants in other cities with comparable Zagat ratings before crowning Sidney Street the standard by which all others should be judged.
